title: The Night Journey and the Ascension
year: Late in the Makkan period — the sirah records six different datings
era: The Journey No One Could Verify
teaser: He described a masjid he had never seen, and a caravan still on the road. One man said: I verify it.

layers.title: The Setting
layers.subtitle: Six datings, and a prayer not yet fixed
layers.content:
Six datings, and the sirah does not settle between them. Al-Mubarakpuri sets them out in order. At-Tabari placed the Night Journey in the same year Allah honoured Muhammad ﷺ with prophethood. An-Nawawi and al-Qurtubi preferred five years after it began. Al-Mansurpuri chose the night of the twenty-seventh of Rajab in the tenth year. Then three later placements: sixteen months before the migration, in Ramadan of the twelfth year of prophethood; one year and two months before it, in al-Muharram of the thirteenth; one year before it, in Rabi'ul-Awwal of the thirteenth.

Reports differ, and al-Mubarakpuri does not pretend otherwise. He notes that the first three have to be read against one fixed point. Khadijah died in Ramadan of the tenth year of prophethood. She died before the five daily prayers were made obligatory, and no one disputes that the five were made obligatory on the night of this journey. His own reading is that the context of Surat al-Isra' places the night very late on the timeline, and he suggests it fell either shortly before the first pledge at al-Aqabah or between the two pledges.

What is not in dispute is the condition of the man it happened to. These were the last days of the Makkan phase, and al-Mubarakpuri describes them as alternating between two extremes: gradual success, and continual persecution.

Prayer, at that point, was not yet what it now is. Ibn Hajar held that the Prophet ﷺ certainly prayed before the Night Journey, while whether it had already been fixed as an obligation remained a matter of controversy; it is related that obligatory prayer stood at twice a day, once in the morning before sunrise and once after sunset. That is the state of the practice on the evening the journey began.
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam, citing Zadul-Ma'ad 2/49 and Ibn Hajar on the ordinance of Salat

layers.title: What Happened
layers.subtitle: A ring in a gate, then one heaven at a time
layers.content:
Ibn al-Qayyim's summary is the spine of the account, and al-Mubarakpuri quotes it. The Prophet ﷺ was carried physically — according to the correct view — from the Sacred Masjid in Makkah to Bait al-Maqdis in Jerusalem, riding al-Buraq in the company of Jibreel. He alighted there, tied the animal to a ring in the gate of the Masjid, and led the prophets in prayer.

Then the ascent, one heaven at a time, and at every level the same exchange: permission sought, a gate opened, a greeting given, a greeting returned, and a prophet bearing witness to his prophethood. In the lowest heaven, Adam, with the souls of the martyrs on his right and the wretched on his left. In the second, Yahya son of Zakariya, and Isa son of Maryam. In the third, Yusuf. In the fourth, Idris. In the fifth, Harun. In the sixth, Musa.

Musa was the only one who wept. Asked why, he answered that he was weeping because he had witnessed a man sent after him who would lead more of his people into Paradise than he himself had led. In the seventh heaven, Ibrahim.

Beyond the seventh he was carried to Sidratul-Muntaha, the farthest lote tree, and shown al-Bait al-Ma'mur, the much-frequented House — circumambulated daily, in the report, by seventy thousand angels, so that an angel who has taken his turn at it does not come round to it again before the Resurrection.

Some of the narrations add that his chest was split open on this occasion too.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim — the hadith of al-Isra' and al-Mi'raj, in the version narrated from Anas bin Malik
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam, quoting Ibn Al-Qayyim, Zadul-Ma'ad 2/47-48

layers.title: The Turning Point
layers.subtitle: Fifty, and the climbs back for less
layers.content:
He was also shown things he would afterwards describe. Malik, the keeper of Hell, with a cheerless frowning face. Paradise, and the Fire. Men who had consumed the property of orphans, with snouts like a camel's, swallowing red-hot stones. Men who had lived off interest, with bellies too big to let them move. Two manifest rivers, the Nile and the Euphrates, and two hidden ones.

But two things were put to him that night as choices, and both of them came home with him.

The first was a drink. He was presented with milk and with wine, and he took the milk. It was said to him: you have chosen the Fitrah — and had you taken the wine, your nation would have been misled.

The second was a number. He was brought near, and Allah ordained fifty prayers a day. On the way down he told Musa. Musa said his followers could not perform so many and sent him back to ask for a decrease. Ten were taken off. He descended, and Musa urged him back. Ten more. Again, and again, at Musa's suggestion, until fifty had become five. Musa told him to ask once more. He would not: 'I feel ashamed now of repeatedly asking my Lord for reduction. I accept and resign to His Will.' As he went on, a Caller was heard saying: 'I have imposed My ordinance and lightened the burden of My servants.'

Notice what that leaves. Everything else on this night could only be reported afterwards — the heavens, the prophets, the lote tree, the seventy thousand angels. The five were not a report. They were an instruction, and they fell on everyone who would ever accept him. The only part of that night any other person can enter is the part that was brought down from fifty.
layers.hadith_ref: The reduction of the prayers from fifty to five — Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, the hadith of al-Isra' and al-Mi'raj
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam, quoting Ibn Al-Qayyim, Zadul-Ma'ad 2/47-48

layers.title: The Revelation
layers.subtitle: One ayah for the journey, and a boundary the scholars kept
layers.content:
The Qur'an gives the journey a single opening verse: «سُبْحَانَ الَّذِي أَسْرَى بِعَبْدِهِ لَيْلًا مِّنَ الْمَسْجِدِ الْحَرَامِ إِلَى الْمَسْجِدِ الْأَقْصَى الَّذِي بَارَكْنَا حَوْلَهُ لِنُرِيَهُ مِنْ آيَاتِنَا» — 'Glorified be He Who took His slave for a journey by night from the Sacred Masjid to the Farthest Masjid, whose surroundings We have blessed, in order that We might show him of Our signs.' (17:1)

Al-Mubarakpuri calls that last clause the most concise justification of the whole journey, and reads it against the pattern set with other prophets: Ibrahim was shown the kingdom of the heavens and the earth so that he would be of those who have faith with certainty (6:75), and Musa was told, 'That We may show you some of Our Greater Signs.' (20:23) Observation is not the equal of information.

Then the surah moves. After the first verse it turns to the deeds of the Jews, and follows that with the admonition that this Qur'an guides to that which is most just and right (17:9), and with a warning about towns destroyed after transgression (17:16-17). Al-Mubarakpuri does not read that order as coincidence.

One thing the revelation did not settle is the very thing a reader most wants settled. Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn Taimiyah record a difference over whether the Prophet ﷺ saw Allah on that night, and the outcome of the research is that seeing Him with the eye is not confirmed as the saying of any of the Companions. The approach in «ثُمَّ دَنَا فَتَدَلَّى» — 'Then he approached and came closer' (53:8) — is Jibreel drawing near, as reported from Aishah and Ibn Mas'ud. And where one narration described a nearness of two bows' length or less, al-Khattabi criticised the wording as a defect of the narrator Sharik: when the same hadith is narrated from Anas without Sharik's chain, those words are not there.
layers.quran_ref: Quran 17:1 — «لِنُرِيَهُ مِنْ آيَاتِنَا» 'in order that We might show him of Our signs'
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim — the hadith of al-Isra' and al-Mi'raj; the wording of the narrator Sharik criticised by Imam al-Khattabi
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam, citing Zadul-Ma'ad 2/47-48 with the footnote of Shu'aib Al-Arnaut 3/35

layers.title: What It Left Behind
layers.subtitle: A title earned at dawn, and an appointment kept daily
layers.content:
In the morning he told them, and the city had a field day. The disbelievers plied him with questions and found the whole thing a convenient way to laugh at the Muslims and their creed. They pressed him for the description of the Masjid in Jerusalem, a place he had never gone, and his answers came back accurate. He told them he had seen the camels of Makkan merchants on the road, coming and going. He directed them to animals of theirs that had strayed. He told them he had drunk some of their water while they slept, and left the container covered.

All of it checked out. Al-Mubarakpuri records that it increased them in nothing but flight from the truth.

The same men went to Abu Bakr with the news, expecting the story to break him. He said: 'Yes, I do verify it.' It was on this occasion that he earned the name As-Siddiq, the one who verifies the truth.

Al-Mubarakpuri reads the night as sitting at the turn of the whole Makkan period. Jerusalem was its first scene, and the message he draws from that is a transfer: the two headquarters of the Ibrahimic faith, the Sacred Masjid in Makkah and the Farthest Masjid in Jerusalem, held in one hand. The verses that followed in the same surah carried an ultimatum to the polytheists and the articles of a community that would own ground of its own — which is why he places the journey close to the pledges that gave the Prophet ﷺ a city.

But the piece of that night which was handed to everybody is smaller than any of that. Before it, by one report, obligatory prayer was twice a day. After it, five. The journey cannot be repeated by anyone. The prayer can be, and it is the only thing brought back from beyond the seventh heaven that was given away to every believer who came afterwards. Most of us treat it as the routine part of the day. It is the surviving fragment of the strangest night in history.
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam, citing Ibn Hisham 1/399, 402-406 and Zadul-Ma'ad 1/48

quiz.prompt: According to the account Ibn al-Qayyim gives, how did the Prophet ﷺ travel from Makkah to Jerusalem that night?

options.text: In a dream, while his body remained in Makkah
Carried physically, riding al-Buraq in the company of Jibreel
On foot over several nights, guided by a light
With a caravan of merchants heading north to Syria

quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar, quoting Ibn Al-Qayyim, Zadul-Ma'ad
quiz.scholar_reflection: Ibn al-Qayyim states the physical journey as the correct view. The detail that fixes it in place is domestic: he tied the animal to a ring in the gate of the Masjid before going in.

quiz.prompt: How many daily prayers were first ordained on that night, and what did they become?

options.text: Five, and they stayed five
Ten, reduced to five
Fifty, reduced in stages to five
Seventeen, one for each rak'ah of the day

quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the hadith of al-Isra' and al-Mi'raj in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim
quiz.scholar_reflection: Ten came off at a time, on Musa's repeated urging. When Musa asked him to go back once more, he said he felt ashamed to keep asking, and stopped at five.

quiz.prompt: He was presented with two things to drink. What was said to him about the choice he made?

options.text: He chose water, and was told it was the drink of the patient
He chose milk, and was told he had chosen the Fitrah — had he taken the wine, his nation would have been misled
He chose honey, and was told it was the drink of Paradise
He refused both, and was told that abstention was better

quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — what the Prophet ﷺ witnessed during al-Isra' and al-Mi'raj
quiz.scholar_reflection: The consequence attached to the choice was not personal. It was national: had he taken the other cup, the report says, his nation would have been misled.

quiz.prompt: Which prophet wept when the Prophet ﷺ met him during the ascent, and why?

options.text: Adam, because he saw the wretched on his left
Ibrahim, because the Sacred House had been given to another nation
Yusuf, because of what his brothers had done to him
Musa, because a man sent after him would lead more of his people into Paradise than he had

quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar, quoting Ibn Al-Qayyim, Zadul-Ma'ad
quiz.scholar_reflection: He is met in the sixth heaven, and he weeps as the Prophet ﷺ leaves. Later that same night, he is the one who keeps sending him back to ask for fewer prayers.

quiz.prompt: What did Abu Bakr say when the disbelievers came to him with the news of the Night Journey?

options.text: That he would wait for a verse to confirm it
That he would ask the Prophet ﷺ privately first
'Yes, I do verify it' — and on this occasion he earned the name As-Siddiq
That the journey must have been a vision rather than a body travelling

quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar, citing Ibn Hisham 1/399
quiz.scholar_reflection: They brought him the story expecting it to be the thing that finally broke his allegiance. It became the reason for the title he is known by.

quiz.prompt: The sirah preserves six different datings for this night and al-Mubarakpuri declines to settle it. How do you take a tradition that keeps its own disagreements on the page?

options.text: Honest transmission is worth more than a tidy chronology
It is uncomfortable, and the discomfort is part of reading real sources
The date matters less because the ruling that came out of the night is undisputed
It shows the transmitters cared about the content and not about dressing it up

quiz.slider_label: How much unresolved detail can you hold without it unsettling you?
quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the views on the date of al-Isra'
quiz.scholar_reflection: At-Tabari, An-Nawawi, Al-Qurtubi and Al-Mansurpuri are all named, and all placed differently. Nobody smoothed the list over.

quiz.prompt: The number was set at fifty and came down to five. What do you take from a command that was made lighter after it was given?

options.text: The lightening was built into the plan, not extracted from it
It shows that asking has a place, even about what has already been decreed
Five is still heavier than most of us actually treat it
The Caller's words settle it: the ordinance is imposed, the burden is lightened

quiz.slider_label: Do you experience the five prayers as a burden or as a lightening?
quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — 'I have imposed My ordinance and lightened the burden of My servants'
quiz.scholar_reflection: He stopped at five out of shame at asking again, not because he was refused. The last ten were still on the table.

quiz.prompt: They asked him to describe a masjid he had never seen. He described it. They checked his account of their own caravans and their own water. It all held, and they disbelieved anyway. What does that tell you about evidence?

options.text: Evidence rarely moves a decision that was made before the evidence arrived
The demand for proof was a way of not deciding, not a way of deciding
The answers were for the people already inclined to listen, not for the questioners
Nothing verifiable is ever enough when the cost of accepting it is a whole way of life

quiz.slider_label: How often do you ask for proof you would not act on?
quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the questioning after the Night Journey, citing Zadul-Ma'ad and Ibn Hisham
quiz.scholar_reflection: He gave them the description of the building, the position of the caravans, and the covered container. Al-Mubarakpuri's summary of the effect is one line: it increased them in nothing but flight from the truth.

quiz.prompt: The scholars stop short of claiming the Prophet ﷺ saw Allah with his eyes, and one narrator's wording about nearness was flagged as a defect. How do you read a tradition that polices its own most dramatic claim?

options.text: Restraint at the highest point is the strongest evidence of care everywhere else
It means the report was handled as testimony, with chains that could be examined
It costs the story some of its drama, and the trade is worth it
It draws a line I should keep too — not going further than the source goes

quiz.slider_label: How willing are you to leave a question open rather than fill it?
quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar, citing Ibn Al-Qayyim and Ibn Taimiyah on whether the Prophet ﷺ saw Allah
quiz.scholar_reflection: Seeing Him with the eye is not confirmed as the saying of a single Companion. The approach in 53:8 is read as Jibreel, on the authority of Aishah and Ibn Mas'ud.

quiz.prompt: Of everything on that night, only one item was handed to every believer who came after: five prayers a day. What do you do with that?

options.text: It is the one part of the night anyone else can enter
A daily habit is what a private miracle was converted into, deliberately
It puts me at the exact point where the number stopped coming down
It means the most ordinary part of my day has the strangest origin in it

quiz.slider_label: Which of your five prayers do you give the least of yourself to?
quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the five prayers made obligatory during the Night Journey
quiz.scholar_reflection: By one report, obligatory prayer had stood at twice a day before that night. The heavens, the prophets and the lote tree could only be reported. The five could be performed.
